title: Minimum Unique Word Abbreviation
statement:
A word is *abbreviated* by picking any number of non-empty substrings that neither overlap nor touch each other and writing each one as its length in decimal (no leading zeros). Because the chosen pieces never touch, two numbers never stand next to each other. For instance, `"window"` can be written as `"window"`, `"w4w"`, `"2nd2"` or `"6"`. The *length* of an abbreviation counts every kept letter as 1 and every number as 1, so `"w4w"` has length 3 and `"2nd2"` has length 4. An abbreviation *matches* a word when it can be produced from that word in this way.

Given a string `target` and a list of strings `dictionary`, return an abbreviation of `target` whose length is as small as possible among those that match no word in `dictionary`. If several abbreviations reach that smallest length, any one of them is accepted. `target` itself never appears in `dictionary`.
constraints: target and every dictionary[i] contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Only dictionary words with the same length as `target` matter: an abbreviation always spans exactly as many characters as its word. Describe an abbreviation of `target` by a bitmask of the positions whose letters are **kept**. For a same-length word, mark in `diff` the positions where it differs from `target`. The abbreviation matches that word exactly when every kept letter agrees with it, so it rules the word out exactly when `mask & diff` is non-zero. The task becomes: find a mask that intersects every `diff` and gives the shortest abbreviation.

The brute force tries every abbreviation in order of length and compares it with each word. The bitmask view is faster, and it allows a search with strong pruning: keeping one more letter never makes an abbreviation shorter, so a branch whose length already reaches the best answer can stop. Keeping a letter where no word differs never helps, so only `candidates` positions are tried.

## Approach

1. Build `diffs` for the words of length `m`, and OR them into `candidates`. With no such word, the answer is just `String(m)`.
2. `lengthOf(mask)` counts kept letters plus the runs of dropped letters, each run being one number.
3. Start with the whole word (`bestMask` all ones, `bestLength = m`), which is always unique because `target` is not in `dictionary`.
4. `search(start, mask)` stops when `mask` is not shorter than the best; records `mask` when it intersects every diff; otherwise tries adding each candidate position from `start` on.
5. Turn `bestMask` back into text: kept letters as they are, each run of skipped letters as its count.

## Example 1, step by step

`target = "apple"`, `dictionary = ["blade"]`. The words differ at positions 0 to 3, so `diffs = [0b01111]` and `candidates = 0b01111`. The empty mask (`"5"`) has length 1 but matches `"blade"`. Adding position 0 gives `"a4"`, length 2, and `0b00001 & 0b01111 != 0`, so it becomes the best. Every other single position gives length 3 (`"1p3"`, `"2p2"`, `"3l1"`) and is pruned, so the answer is `"a4"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(2^m · (m + n)) in the worst case, which the constraint `log2(n) + m <= 21` keeps near 2^21 · m; pruning makes it far smaller in practice. Building `diffs` costs O(n · m).
- Space: O(n) for `diffs`, plus O(m) recursion depth.

## Pitfalls

- Words of another length can never match, so they must not block anything.
- An abbreviation's length counts a whole number as 1, so `"a10"` has length 2, not 3.
- Return the full word when nothing shorter works; that is valid because `target` is not in `dictionary`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `m` | length of `target` |
| `diffs` | one bitmask per same-length word: positions where it differs from `target` |
| `candidates` | OR of all `diffs`: the only positions worth keeping |
| `mask` | positions of `target` kept as letters in the abbreviation being tried |
| `bestMask`, `bestLength` | the shortest unique abbreviation found and its length |
| `skipped` | length of the current run of dropped letters while building `result` |

narration.6: Look only at words as long as target; a word of another length can never match.
narration.9: Set bit i wherever this word's letter differs from target's.
narration.12: Any position where some word differs is a candidate to keep.
narration.14: No same-length word: one number covering the whole word is already unique.
narration.19: Bit i of the mask says whether target[i] is kept as a letter.
narration.20: A dropped letter opens a new number when it starts the word or follows a kept letter.
narration.21: Each kept letter and each number adds 1 to the length.
narration.26: Start from the whole word, which is always unique because target is not in dictionary.
narration.30: Keeping more letters never shortens an abbreviation, so stop once this one is not shorter than the best.
narration.31: The mask keeps a differing letter of every same-length word, so no word matches it.
narration.32: Record it as the new shortest unique abbreviation.
narration.36: Otherwise try keeping one more position, in increasing order so each set is built once.
narration.37: Only candidate positions can rule a word out; recurse with that position kept.
narration.45: A kept position ends the current run of dropped letters.
narration.46: Write the run's length as one number before the letter.
narration.50: A dropped letter extends the current run.
narration.53: A run that reaches the end of the word also becomes a number.
narration.54: Return the shortest abbreviation that no dictionary word matches.
